RESPONSE:
# Points Recalled from "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team"

This is from memory. Wording is paraphrased unless in quotation marks, and I've marked places where I'm unsure.

## Opening
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice is what slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned
- Every claim has earned a certain weight, whether it comes from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes.
- Weight comes partly from the evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Experience is one way a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues with years in an area have usually been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, because it reflects checks they have already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly, but they are not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is "more insidious".
- A newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- **Example:** A colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports that its defect rate fell after a process change. Take this as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer
- Show you've taken in a message by restating its main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it.
- This isn't politeness; it keeps the conversation moving forward rather than circling.
- Start from what you agree with: find the part that's right, say so, and extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement put people on the defensive and cost time.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step.
- **Example:** A manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. The reply confirms the direction, picks up the actionable points, and says the budget will follow "in due course".

## 3. Go to the source
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has already been through the source, usually by someone who knows the area better than you.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go back to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and can signal distrust of colleagues.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into "private versions of the truth" and stops being able to act.
- **Example:** Team notes summarise a report as "costs fell 12%". Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

## 4. Do not leave open what can be closed
- Mark which questions the evidence settles and which it leaves uncertain, then keep the work moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on. It can be revisited later.
- A question left hanging tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping questions open because one more check feels safer, is said to be more common in careful people. It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed and save your energy for live questions.
- **Example:** A trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Handle problems there as they arise.

## 5. Help the colleague who sees differently
- New colleagues and those from other parts of the organisation see things differently. That's valuable only if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team knows.
- When asking for a check, give context: what you've concluded, where you think the risks are, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster.
- In reverse, as the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well-founded and the moment is right.
- A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.
- *(I don't recall a separate worked example in this section.)*

## 6. Make your moves where they will land well
- Before taking a next step you can see, check that it fits what the owners of the area have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating them. Make the call once direction is confirmed. Release results when they're ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework; surprising decisions often have to be unpicked and redone.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your position; the owner can see things you can't. Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This isn't a licence to wait indefinitely. Small, routine steps don't need sign-off.
- Steps that matter usually affect others, so the default is to check first and then act together.
- **Example:** Rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether they'd like it restructured, and how.

## 7. Failures come in pairs
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other.
- The six pairs:
  1. **Overclaiming / second-guessing:** overstating a provisional result; casting doubt on an established one.
  2. **Inventing a flaw / overlooking one:** finding a non-existent problem to look rigorous; missing a real one.
  3. **Closing too early / keeping open too long:** declaring a question answered before it is; refusing to accept the team's answer.
  4. **Abandoning a line / relitigating one:** dropping an agreed approach at the first difficulty; reopening a decided one.
  5. **Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively:** accepting anything said; disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded.
  6. **Acting alone / waiting too long:** making calls others should have shaped; delaying steps already agreed.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, "the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one."

## A last word
- The note isn't a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, and an agreed direction.
- "Trust those. They are how good work gets done together."
